read.sections.0.heading.source: A model learns from labelled examples
read.sections.0.heading.back: A model learns from labelled examples

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI learns a bit like studying with flashcards. At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data: pictures of leaves, each with the correct answer, called a label, either “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses these examples to build a model. It uses the model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen. This is machine learning. Nobody writes the rule “spots mean sick”; the computer finds patterns like that in the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, one kind of machine learning. It is an old idea. A machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards in 1958, and researchers studied this lesson's method in 1967. It became far more useful after 2010, with more data and faster computers.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI learns in a way a bit like studying with flashcards. At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data: pictures of leaves, each with the correct answer, called a label, either “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses these examples to build a model. The computer uses that model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen. This is machine learning. Nobody writes the rule “spots mean sick”; the computer itself finds patterns like that in the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, one kind of machine learning. This is an old idea. A machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards in 1958, and researchers studied the method in this lesson in 1967. This method became much more useful after 2010, with more data and faster computers.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Supervised learning" as "pembelajaran terawasi", the usual term in Indonesian computing books; "pembelajaran terbimbing" is also used. "Flashcards" as "kartu hafalan" (memorising cards).

read.sections.0.simpler.source: At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data. Each leaf picture has the right answer, called a label: “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses them to make a model. It uses the model to guess. This is machine learning. Nobody tells it “spots mean sick”. It finds that in the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. It is an old idea. A machine did it in 1958. This method was studied in 1967. It grew more useful after 2010.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data. Every leaf picture has the correct answer, called a label: “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses them to make a model. The computer uses that model to guess. This is machine learning. Nobody says “spots mean sick”. The computer finds it by itself in the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. This is an old idea. A machine did it in 1958. This method was studied in 1967. This method became more useful after 2010.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Better examples, then a fair test
read.sections.1.heading.back: Better examples, then a fair test

read.sections.1.text.source: The first model learned from only two examples. It guesses in a simple way: it finds the example most like the new leaf and copies its label. On six new leaves it got four right. It called a small, light green leaf “sick”, because it had too few examples to compare with. Then the team added four leaves that looked different, and it got all six right. But the team had already looked at those six test leaves while they improved the model. A fair test uses leaves that nobody has used yet. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three of them right. It called a long leaf that was turning yellow “healthy”. A fresh test shows what a model still gets wrong. Four leaves are still a small test.
read.sections.1.text.back: The first model learned from only two examples. This model guesses in a simple way: it looks for the example most similar to the new leaf, then copies its label. Of six new leaves, the model guessed four correctly. It called a small light green leaf “sick”, because it had too few examples to compare. Then the team added four leaves that looked different, and the model guessed all six correctly. But the team had already seen those six test leaves while they were improving the model. A fair test uses leaves nobody has used yet. The team set aside four leaves. The model guessed three of them correctly. It called a long leaf that was starting to turn yellow “healthy”. A new test shows what the model still guesses wrongly. Four leaves are still a small test.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The first model had only two examples. It finds the example most like a new leaf. It copies that label. It got four of six new leaves right. It had too few examples. Then the team added four different leaves. Now it got all six right. But the team had already seen those six leaves. A fair test uses new leaves. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three of them right. A new test shows what it still gets wrong.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: The first model had only two examples. The model looks for the example most like a new leaf. It copies that label. It was right on four of six new leaves. There were too few examples. Then the team added four different leaves. Now the model was right on all six. But the team had already seen those six leaves. A fair test uses new leaves. The team set aside four leaves. The model was right on three of them. A new test shows what is still wrong.

read.sections.2.text.source: Real tools work in a similar way, at a much bigger size. In Tanzania, researchers from the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Penn State University made a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from pictures of the leaves of cassava, a food crop, taken in Tanzanian fields, and it works without the internet. When researchers tested it on plants in the field, it did much better when it looked at six leaves from a plant than at one. Relevant examples with correct labels help a model. More examples alone do not always help: a wrong label can make guesses worse. And a tool like this only helps people check leaves. Farmers and experts still decide what to do.
read.sections.2.text.back: Real tools work in a similar way, at a much bigger size. In Tanzania, researchers from the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Penn State University made a free phone app called Nuru. The app learned from pictures of cassava leaves, a food crop, taken in Tanzanian fields, and the app works without the internet. When researchers tested it on plants in the field, the result was much better when the app looked at six leaves from one plant than at only one leaf. Relevant examples with correct labels help a model. More examples alone do not always help: a wrong label can make guesses worse. And a tool like this only helps people check leaves. Farmers and experts are still the ones who decide what to do.
read.sections.2.text.note: The institute's name is kept in English with an Indonesian gloss in brackets on first use. Cassava is "singkong", which Indonesian learners know well; the simpler text still explains it, as the English does.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Real tools work like this too, but they are much bigger. In Tanzania, researchers made a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from pictures of cassava leaves. A wrong label can make it worse. The app helps people check leaves. People still decide what to do.

watch.summary.source: This video explains computer vision. Computer vision is how a computer finds meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture like you do. It sees a number for each tiny dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, like the letter X, does not work well, because people draw an X in many ways. With machine learning, the computer learns from many labelled examples instead. It is like learning with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer and slowly gets better. Harder pictures, like faces, need bigger models. The video shows farm robots that tell crops from weeds. It also warns about a problem. If the training data leaves some people out, the tool can fail for them. So training data must be large and varied.
watch.summary.back: This video explains computer vision. Computer vision is how a computer finds meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture like you. A computer sees one number for each very small dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, like the letter X, does not work well, because people draw an X in many ways. With machine learning, the computer learns from many labelled examples. This is like learning with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer, and slowly becomes better. Harder pictures, like faces, need bigger models. The video shows farm robots that tell crops from weeds. The video also warns about a problem. If the training data does not include some people, the tool can fail for them. So training data must be large and varied.

educatorNotes.1.source: The model is deliberately simple: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label of the most similar example. It is one supervised method; Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is far bigger, and other kinds of machine learning don't need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing are the same.
educatorNotes.1.back: The model is deliberately simple: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label of the most similar example. It is one supervised learning method; Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is far bigger, and other kinds of machine learning don't need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing stay the same.

educatorNotes.2.source: Nuru: the evaluation in Tanzania (Mrisho and others, a bioRxiv preprint from 2020) found the app more accurate with six leaves per plant than with one leaf image. The lesson gives no percentages on purpose: the study's numbers depend on which test and which disease. The app supports diagnosis; it does not replace extension workers or farmers' decisions.

educatorNotes.3.source: If a learner labels an example differently from the gardener in the extension, the model follows the learner. That is a good moment to ask: who decides the right label?
